01.note: The Sages said that Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai would take a myrtle branch and dance before a bride, calling out: A fair and attractive bride. Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak went further and juggled three branches as he danced, and Rabbi Zeira complained that the old man was humiliating them. When Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak died, a pillar of fire separated him from everyone else, a sign the tradition says is given to only one or two people in a generation. Rabbi Zeira then said that the old man's branch had served him well; others report that he said his nonsense, or his method, had served him well.
01.why: The discussion has been collecting the songs sung to praise brides and newly ordained Sages; this story turns to how far a Sage may go to bring joy to a bride, and is followed by Rav Aha, who danced with a bride on his shoulders.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai
people.about: A Sage who danced before brides holding a myrtle branch.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak
people.about: An old Sage who juggled three myrtle branches while dancing before brides.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who first objected to the juggling, then said it had earned the old man his honor.

terms.meaning: A fragrant green branch, carried here as part of the celebration in front of the bride.
A heavenly sign of honor; by the tradition the Gemara cites, it marks off only one or two people in a generation.

02.note: Abaye's tenant farmer asked him whether he could betroth a nursing woman fifteen months after her child was born. Abaye said yes, piling up reasons: the law usually follows Rabbi Yehuda, the earlier school of Beit Hillel held the shorter wait, and Ulla and Mar Ukva had both permitted it. When Abaye told his teacher Rav Yosef, Rav Yosef quoted Rav and Shmuel: she must wait twenty-four months even before betrothal. Abaye ran three parasangs after the farmer (some say one parasang through sand) but could not catch him. He drew the lesson that one should not rule even on something as simple as eating an egg in a milk dish near one's teacher, because one will not get it right.
02.why: A teaching of the Sages says a nursing widow must wait before remarrying, with opinions ranging from 24 to 18 months; the story shows the shorter wait being relied on in practice and then overturned by Rav and Shmuel's stricter ruling.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who gave a lenient ruling to his tenant farmer and later regretted it.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Abaye's teacher, who told him Rav and Shmuel required a 24-month wait.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A Sage who ruled that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda's shorter wait.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: A Sage who said Rabbi Hanina allowed him to marry a nursing woman after fifteen months.

terms.meaning: Here, a widow still nursing her baby; the Sages made her wait before remarrying so a new pregnancy would not cut off the child's milk.
A Persian unit of distance, a long walk of several kilometers.
Two early schools of Sages that often disagreed; the law usually follows Beit Hillel.

03.note: Two deeds of sale for the same field came before Rav Yosef. One said the field was sold on the fifth of Nisan; the other said only that it was sold in Nisan. Rav Yosef gave the field to the holder of the dated deed, telling the other man that his deed could have been written as late as the twenty-ninth. The loser then asked for a court document letting him collect from land the seller sold from the first of Iyyar onward. Rav Yosef refused, because any buyer could answer: your deed may be from the first of Nisan, so the field you bought really is yours; go take it back from the other man.
03.why: The Gemara has just told of two deeds to one property written on the same day, where Rav Sheshet and Rav Nahman ruled differently; this is a further case of competing deeds, and afterwards the Gemara explains how the two holders could protect themselves.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The judge before whom the two conflicting deeds were brought.

terms.meaning: A written record of a sale; its date matters because the earlier buyer has the stronger claim.
A court document allowing a creditor or buyer to seize property the debtor had sold or pledged.
Land that stands as security for a debt, so it can be taken from a later buyer if the debt is not paid.

04.note: On the day Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was dying, the Sages declared a fast and prayed for him, threatening to stab with a sword anyone who said he had died. His maidservant went up to the roof and first prayed that those below would prevail over those above; but seeing him suffer, going in and out of the bathroom and taking his phylacteries off and on, she prayed the opposite. When the Sages would not stop praying, she threw a jug from the roof; in the moment of silence, he died. Bar Kappara, sent to check, told the Sages in a parable that angels had captured the sacred ark, leaving them to say the word themselves. As he died, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi raised his ten fingers and said he had toiled in Torah without enjoying the world, and a Divine Voice answered: He enters in peace.
04.why: The Gemara has been discussing where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi lay ill, in Tzippori rather than Beit She'arim; it goes on to tell the day of his death, and afterwards explains the verse the Divine Voice quoted.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The great Sage whose death is told here.

people.name: bar Kappara
people.about: A Sage sent to check on Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who broke the news in a parable.

terms.meaning: Small leather boxes holding verses of the Torah, worn on the head and arm and removed before entering a bathroom.
A voice from Heaven announcing God's judgment.
Heaven, which wanted the dying Sage, and the people on earth, who prayed to keep him.

05.note: Rav Hiyya Arikha's mother-in-law was also his brother's widow. She lived in her father's house, and for twenty-five years he supported her from his brother's estate. Then he told her she had lost the right to both support and her marriage-contract payment. She took him to Rabba bar Sheila, who ruled that she had not claimed out of embarrassment at his respectful treatment, and ordered him to pay. When he refused, Rabba bar Sheila wrote her a document letting her seize his property, and Rava upheld the ruling. But when she asked Rava for the produce of that property, he found the document did not state that the land came from her late husband's estate, so it was flawed and gave her no right to the produce.
05.why: The mishna says a widow living in her father's house may always collect her marriage contract, but one in her husband's house loses it after twenty-five years; this case tests that rule on a widow treated with respect while in her father's house.

people.name: Rav Hiyya Arikha
people.about: Supported his widowed sister-in-law, who was also his mother-in-law, then refused to pay her marriage contract.

people.name: Rabba bar Sheila
people.about: The judge who ordered Rav Hiyya Arikha to pay and wrote her a seizure document.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who upheld the ruling but found the seizure document faulty.

terms.meaning: The ketuba, a document promising a wife a sum of money from her husband's property if he dies or divorces her.
Food and support owed to a widow from her late husband's estate until she collects her marriage contract.
A court document allowing a creditor to seize specific property in payment.
The crops and income a property yields, which belong to whoever owns it at the time.

06.note: A man betrothed a woman with a blue marble stone, and Rav Hisda checked whether it was worth a peruta. The man's mother said it had been worth a peruta on the day of the betrothal, but Rav Hisda said she could not make the woman forbidden to another man. He compared it to Yehudit, Rabbi Hiyya's wife, who suffered painful childbirths and claimed her mother said she had been betrothed to someone else as a child; Rabbi Hiyya told her that her mother could not forbid her to him. When the Sages pointed out that there were witnesses in Idit who knew the stone's value that day, Rav Hisda answered that they were not here.
06.why: Shmuel had ruled that a betrothal with a cheap item may still count, since it might be worth a peruta elsewhere; the Gemara shows Rav Hisda rejecting that view. Afterwards Abaye and Rava disagree, and the Sages avoided marrying into the woman's family.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The judge who ruled on the betrothal with the blue marble stone.

people.name: Yehudit
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's wife, who suffered painful childbirths and wished to leave him.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Yehudit's husband, who told her that her mother's claim could not forbid her to him.

terms.meaning: The smallest coin; an object given for betrothal must be worth at least this much.
The first stage of Jewish marriage, made by giving the woman something of value; after it she is bound to the man and forbidden to others.

07.note: Rabbi Yehuda from India was a convert who had no heirs. When he fell ill, Mar Zutra came to visit him, and when he saw that the sick man was about to die, he told the man's slave: Take off my shoes and carry them to my house. By having the slave serve him, Mar Zutra meant to claim the slave as soon as the owner died. Some say the slave was an adult, and the Gemara sums up: one departed to death, and the other departed to life.
07.why: The discussion has just said a master acquires a slave when the slave does work for him, such as lifting him; Mar Zutra uses that method. Afterwards the Gemara asks whether, if the slave was a minor, he even needed to hurry.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda from India
people.about: A convert with no heirs, who was dying.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: A Sage who visited him and acquired his slave before he died.

terms.meaning: When a convert with no Jewish heirs dies, his property is ownerless, and the first person to take possession of it acquires it.

08.note: Rav Yosef said that if Aher, the former Sage Elisha ben Avuya, had read the verse "that it may go well with you" as referring to the World-to-Come, as his grandson Rabbi Ya'akov did, he would not have sinned. The Gemara asks what made him sin. Some say he saw a son climb to a roof at his father's command, send away a mother bird as the Torah requires, and then die. Others say he saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator, who had been executed by the government, lying in the street and being dragged by a pig, and said: Shall a mouth that produced pearls lap up dirt? For this he went out and sinned.
08.why: The Gemara has been defending Rabbi Ya'akov's teaching that the reward for mitzvot comes in the World-to-Come, not in this world, citing a son who died returning from exactly these mitzvot; Aher is the one who drew the opposite conclusion.

people.name: Aher
people.about: Literally Other, the name given to the former Sage Elisha ben Avuya after he sinned.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov
people.about: Aher's daughter's son, who taught that the promised reward is in the World-to-Come.

people.name: Hutzpit the disseminator
people.about: A Sage executed by the government, whose tongue Aher saw in the street.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who says Aher would not have sinned had he read the verse as Rabbi Ya'akov did.

terms.meaning: The life after this one, where, in Rabbi Ya'akov's teaching, the reward for mitzvot is paid.
A Torah commandment to send off the mother before taking eggs or chicks from a nest; like honoring parents, it is promised long life.
The person who repeated a Sage's lecture aloud so the whole audience could hear it.

09.note: A blind man used to review mishnayot with Mar Shmuel. One day he was late, so Mar Shmuel sent a messenger to bring him. The two missed each other on different roads, and the messenger reached the blind man's house. He came back and reported that he had seen the man's wife committing adultery. The blind man asked Mar Shmuel what to do, and Mar Shmuel told him: If this messenger is trusted by you, go and divorce her; if not, do not divorce her.
09.why: Abaye and Rava disagree whether a single witness is believed when he says a man's wife committed adultery; Abaye tells this case as his proof, and Rava answers that Mar Shmuel meant trusted like two witnesses.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who tells this case as proof for his view.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: The teacher with whom the blind man reviewed mishnayot, who answered his question.

terms.meaning: Teachings of the Mishna, the earliest written collection of Jewish law, which students memorized and reviewed aloud.

10.note: Giddul bar Re'ilai sent a bill of divorce to his wife by an agent. The agent found her sitting and weaving and told her: This is your bill of divorce. She said: Go away for now and come back tomorrow to give it to me. When the agent reported this to Giddul bar Re'ilai, he said: Blessed is He Who is good and does good, glad that the divorce had not been delivered.
10.why: Abaye and Rava go on to disagree about this very case: whether a husband who shows he does not want the divorce delivered, without cancelling it outright, has made it void.

people.name: Giddul bar Re'ilai
people.about: A man who sent his wife a bill of divorce and was relieved when it was not delivered.

terms.meaning: The get, the document a husband gives his wife to end the marriage; the divorce takes effect only when she receives it.

terms.term: Blessed is He Who is good and does good
terms.meaning: A blessing said on hearing good news.

11.note: Rav Sheizevi said that a thief who slaughters a stolen, consecrated animal outside the Temple is liable to karet by rabbinic law. The people who heard him laughed: is there such a thing as karet by rabbinic law? Rava told them: A great man has spoken; do not laugh at him. He explained that Rav Sheizevi meant karet that comes about through the words of the Sages, who declared the thief's consecration valid and so placed the animal in his possession.
11.why: The Gemara is asking whether a thief can consecrate a stolen animal, given a teaching that makes him liable to karet for slaughtering it outside the Temple; Rav Sheizevi's remark answers that difficulty, and Rava then asks from when the animal became the thief's.

people.name: Rav Sheizevi
people.about: A Sage whose explanation was laughed at.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who defended Rav Sheizevi and explained what he meant.

terms.meaning: Literally cutting off: a punishment from Heaven for certain grave sins, including sacrificing an offering outside the Temple.
To dedicate an animal to the Temple as an offering, which only its owner can do.

12.note: When Rabba bar Avuh was ill, Rav Huna and Rav Nahman went to visit him. Rav Huna asked Rav Nahman to ask the sick man whether the law follows Rabbi Yosei. Rav Nahman objected that he did not even know Rabbi Yosei's reason, and Rav Huna promised to explain it afterwards. Rav Nahman asked, and Rabba bar Avuh answered that Rav had ruled the law follows Rabbi Yosei. When they left, Rav Huna told Rav Nahman the reason: Rabbi Yosei holds that the date written in a document shows when it takes effect.
12.why: The Gemara is testing the idea that Rav Huna was unsure whether the law follows Rabbi Yosei; this visit shows he accepted Rav's ruling that it does, so the Gemara concludes his doubt must be about something narrower.

people.name: Rabba bar Avuh
people.about: A sick Sage who reported Rav's ruling.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who visited him and wanted to know the law.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage who visited with Rav Huna and asked the question for him.

terms.term: the date in a document shows when it takes effect
terms.meaning: Rabbi Yosei's principle: a dated bill of divorce takes effect from the date written on it, even if a condition is fulfilled later.

13.note: A man sold land and promised to cover the buyer for any unavoidable accident that might happen to it. Then a river was diverted through the land. The buyer brought a claim before Ravina, who told the seller to pay him, since he had accepted that responsibility. Rav Aha bar Tahalifa objected that this was an uncommon accident, which the promise did not cover. The case came before Rava, who agreed that the seller did not have to pay. Ravina challenged Rava from a teaching about a conditional bill of divorce; Rava's reply comes in the discussion that follows.
13.why: The Gemara has been discussing conditional divorces where the husband dies by an unexpected cause such as a collapsing house or a snake; this sale raises the same question of whether a condition covers rare accidents, and Ravina challenges Rava from that teaching.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The judge who first ordered the seller to pay.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Tahalifa
people.about: A Sage who argued that the promise did not cover so rare an accident.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled that the seller need not pay.

terms.meaning: Damage no one could have prevented; the question here is whether a seller's promise covers even rare events of this kind.
The get, the document that ends a marriage; it may be given on a condition, such as the husband not recovering from an illness.

14.note: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok recalled studying with Rabbi Yohanan the Horani, a disciple of Beit Shammai, who in years of drought ate dry bread with salt. Rabbi Elazar's father sent him olives, but Rabbi Yohanan saw they were moist with their own juice, which could make them susceptible to ritual impurity, and politely said: I do not eat olives. When Rabbi Elazar told his father, the father sent word that the barrel had been perforated and then clogged by sediment, so the olives had not become susceptible. The text does not say what Rabbi Yohanan did next.
14.why: The Gemara is asking whether Beit Shammai actually practised by their own rulings where they disagreed with Beit Hillel; the teaching adds that Rabbi Yohanan the Horani always followed Beit Hillel, which is praise only if Beit Shammai's followers usually followed their own view.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok
people.about: The teller, who studied with Rabbi Yohanan the Horani and brought him olives from his father.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan the Horani
people.about: A disciple of Beit Shammai who lived on bread and salt in years of drought.

terms.meaning: Food can become ritually impure only after it has been made wet by certain liquids, such as olive oil, with the owner's consent.
A barrel with a hole bored in it to let the olive juice drain out, showing the owner did not want the juice on the olives.
Two early schools of Sages that often disagreed; the law usually follows Beit Hillel.

15.note: When Rav came to the town of Dardeshir, he made a public announcement: Which woman will be my wife for the day? Rav Nahman did the same when he came to Shakhnetziv. Both Sages, away from home, publicly sought a wife for the length of their stay.
15.why: Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov taught that a man should not marry wives in different countries, lest his children meet and unknowingly marry each other; the Gemara asks how these Sages could do so, and answers that a Sage's children are always known as his.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who sought a wife for the day when visiting Dardeshir.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage who did the same when visiting Shakhnetziv.

16.note: Rabbi Elazar taught a ruling of Rabbi Yohanan in the study hall without naming him, and Rabbi Yohanan was angry. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi tried to calm him by recalling how Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei once argued in a Tiberias synagogue until a Torah scroll tore, and Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma predicted the synagogue would become a place of idol worship, as it did. That made Rabbi Yohanan angrier: were they now making him and his student colleagues? Then Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi pointed out that Joshua taught without saying Moses told me, yet everyone knew it was Moses' Torah; so too everyone knew Rabbi Elazar's teaching came from Rabbi Yohanan. Rabbi Yohanan was appeased and asked the other two why they could not appease him that way.
16.why: The Gemara has just explained a ruling about levirate marriage that Rabbi Elazar taught without naming Rabbi Yohanan; afterwards it explains his anger: when a teaching is repeated in a scholar's name, his lips move in the grave.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Rabbi Elazar's teacher, angered that his ruling was taught without his name.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: Rabbi Yohanan's beloved disciple, who taught the ruling without naming him.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: With Rabbi Asi, tried and failed to calm Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: With Rabbi Ami, tried and failed to calm Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi
people.about: The Sage who succeeded in appeasing Rabbi Yohanan.

terms.meaning: Things set aside from use on Shabbat, which may not be moved; the question was whether a door bolt counted as a usable vessel or as raw material.
The house of study where the Sages taught and debated.

17.note: In the town of Neresh, a woman had been betrothed as a minor and then came of age. Her husband seated her in the bridal chair under the marriage canopy, but before they had been together, another man came, seized her from him, and married her. Rav's students Rav Bruna and Rav Hananel were there, and they did not require her to receive a bill of divorce from the second man.
17.why: The Gemara is checking Rav's view that a marriage to a girl betrothed as a minor is complete only after intercourse once she is an adult; this case seems to contradict it, and Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi then explain it away.

people.name: Rav Bruna
people.about: A student of Rav, present at the incident.

people.name: Rav Hananel
people.about: A student of Rav, present at the incident.

terms.meaning: A young girl could be married off by her family before adulthood; the Sages debate whether that marriage is fully binding once she grows up.
The get, the document needed to end a valid marriage; not requiring one means the second marriage never took effect.

18.note: Rav Yitzhak bar Bisna lost the keys to the study hall in the public domain, and on Shabbat no one could carry them back. He asked Rabbi Pedat what to do. Rabbi Pedat told him to take boys and girls to walk where the keys were lost: if they found the keys, they would bring them of their own accord, without anyone telling them to.
18.why: From Rabbi Pedat's advice the Gemara infers that a court need not stop a child from breaking a prohibition, and then tests that idea against other teachings about children and gentiles on Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak bar Bisna
people.about: The man who lost the keys to the study hall.

people.name: Rabbi Pedat
people.about: The Sage who advised him to let children find the keys.

terms.meaning: Open public space such as a street; on Shabbat it is forbidden to carry objects there.
A child not yet obligated in the commandments; the question is whether adults must stop children who break them.

19.note: Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Yonatan were walking in a cemetery, and the blue string of Rabbi Yonatan's ritual fringes was dragging over the graves. Rabbi Hiyya told him to lift it, so the dead would not say: Tomorrow they will be buried with us, and now they insult us. Rabbi Yonatan asked whether the dead know so much, quoting "the dead know nothing." Rabbi Hiyya answered that he had not read or understood the verse properly: "the living" who know they will die are the righteous, who are called living even in death. His explanation continues in the discussion that follows.
19.why: The Gemara is discussing the honor owed to the dead, such as not riding on their bones and escorting a funeral; this story asks whether the dead even know how they are treated.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage who told his companion to lift his fringes so as not to insult the dead.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan
people.about: A Sage whose fringes dragged over the graves, and who doubted the dead know anything.

terms.meaning: Tzitzit, the knotted strings worn on the corners of a garment as a commandment, which included a sky-blue thread.

20.note: A student asked Rabbi Yehoshua whether the evening prayer is optional (optional, he said) and then Rabban Gamliel, the Nasi (obligatory). Before the assembled Sages, Rabban Gamliel made Rabbi Yehoshua admit his view and left him standing through the lecture. The angry crowd halted the lecture and removed Rabban Gamliel, appointing eighteen-year-old Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, whose hair miraculously turned white. The doors opened to all students and hundreds of benches were added. Rabban Gamliel stayed in the study hall, then went to apologize; at Rabbi Yehoshua's soot-blackened house he learned he was a blacksmith. Forgiven for his father's sake, he was restored, lecturing three weeks to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's one.
20.why: The mishna says the evening prayer is not fixed, which the Gemara reads as optional, the very point Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua disputed; this teaching tells the confrontation that dispute led to.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Nasi, head of the Sages, removed from office after humiliating Rabbi Yehoshua.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: The Sage who held the evening prayer optional and was made to stand; a blacksmith by trade.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Appointed head of the yeshiva in Rabban Gamliel's place at eighteen.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage considered for the post, who later offered to restore Rabban Gamliel.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: The student whose question set off the whole incident.

terms.meaning: The president and leader of the Sages and of the community.
A name for the Torah scholars who do battle in debate in the study hall.
The person who repeated a Sage's lecture aloud so the whole audience could hear it.
Being allowed to marry a Jew by birth; the Torah forbids this to Ammonite converts.
